title: Social Security Legislation Amendment (Further Strengthening Job Seeker Compliance) Bill 2015
short_title: Social Security Legislation Amendment (Further Strengthening Job Seeker Compliance) Bill 2015

divisions.question: Julie Collins I thank those members who contributed to the debate, particularly the members from this side, who, I know, are very passionate about this part of policy. As I said in my contribution on the second reading, there are some aspects of this bill that Labor is prepared to support—those amendments that more closely align the date of noncompliance to penalties and/or suspensions—but we are not prepared to support some of the harsher measures in this bill that could further disadvantage vulnerable job seekers. Labor is looking forward to the report on this bill from the Senate committee in late November and the evidence from stakeholders on how they believe the bill will operate. I am pleased to hear the minister's comments that the government is seriously looking at the amendments that Labor has put forward and will negotiate with Labor on the bill. Given that Labor will not be supporting some of the harsher measures, which we believe will not assist job seekers, I seek leave to move amendments (1) to (19), as circulated in my name, together. Leave granted. I move opposition amendments (1) to (19) together: (1) Schedule 1, items 10 to 16, page 4 (line 25) to page 5 (line 31), omit the items. (2) Schedule 1, item 18, page 6 (lines 7 to 12), omit the item, substitute: 18 Paragraph 42SA(1)(c) Repeal the paragraph. (3) Schedule 1, item 19, page 6 (line 15), omit "Note 1", substitute "Note". (4) Schedule 1, item 19, page 6 (line 16), omit note 2. (5) Schedule 1, item 22, page 7 (table item 1), omit the table item. (6) Schedule 1, item 22, page 8 (table item 6), omit the table item. (7) Schedule 1, item 31, page 9 (lines 13 to 15), omit the item. (8) Schedule 1, item 34, page 9 (line 24) to page 10 (line 10), omit the item. (9) Schedule 1, item 35, page 10 (lines 14 and 15), omit "or to entry into employment pathway plans". (10) Schedule 1, item 36, page 10 (lines 18 and 19), omit "or to entry into employment pathway plans". (11) Schedule 1, items 38 and 39, page 1
Ian Goodenough The question now is that this bill be agreed to.

speeches.speaker: Luke Hartsuyker
speeches.brief: The bill introduces immediate payment suspensions and penalties for job seekers who refuse a job plan, behave inappropriately at appointments, miss appointments with specialist providers, or fail to adequately search for work, and removes waivers for refusing suitable work, resulting in an eight-week non-payment period. It builds on 2014 reforms that increased rescheduled appointment attendance from 65% to over 90% and reduced average payment suspension duration by 40%.

speeches.speaker: Stephen Jones
speeches.brief: The member opposed the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Further Strengthening Job Seeker Compliance) Bill 2015, supporting the second reading amendment and labelling the bill "Work Choices on water." He argued it would enable the wholesale sacking of Australian maritime workers, drive down wages, and replace them with foreign workers, comparing it to the Peter Reith and John Howard-led Patrick waterfront dispute.

speeches.speaker: Julie Collins
speeches.brief: Labor will support measures that immediately suspend payments for failing to participate in activities or job search, but opposes removing the waiver for eight-week penalties for refusing work, immediate suspension for not signing a job plan, and a new power to penalise 'inappropriate behaviour'. Labor will not support the bill without amendments, noting that 78% of eight-week penalties were waived in 2013-14 and only 0.2% of job seekers received such penalties.

speeches.speaker: Karen McNamara
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Further Strengthening Job Seeker Compliance) Bill 2015, which introduces immediate penalties for job seekers who fail to enter an employment pathway plan, refuse suitable job offers, or do not engage in job-seeking activities, building on 2014 reforms that increased second appointment attendance from 65% to over 90%. The bill also simplifies the compliance framework and takes effect from 1 July 2016.

speeches.speaker: Karen McNamara
speeches.brief: The bill simplifies job seeker compliance by renaming short-term financial penalties as "no-show no-pay failures," maintains existing protections for vulnerable job seekers, and is backed by $6.8 billion over four years for employment support and $24.5 million for the reforms. It reinforces that income support requires fulfilling mutual obligations to seek work.

speeches.speaker: Jill Hall
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Further Strengthening Job Seeker Compliance) Bill 2015, arguing it punishes job seekers without considering individual circumstances—citing examples of unfair payment suspensions for a car breakdown and a funeral, and an unsuitable referral of a person with a criminal record to an aged-care facility in the Shortland electorate—and called for protecting job seekers' rights to review and reasonable excuse.

speeches.speaker: John Cobb
speeches.brief: The speech argued for the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Further Strengthening Job Seeker Compliance) Bill 2015, introducing immediate payment suspensions and penalties for job seekers who refuse an Employment Pathway Plan, behave badly at appointments, or fail to adequately search for work. It cited that attendance at reconnection appointments rose from 65% in 2013-14 to over 90% in June 2015 after earlier reforms.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Broad
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Further Strengthening Job Seeker Compliance) Bill 2015 is necessary to impose obligations on unemployed benefit recipients, including penalties for failing to enter an Employment Pathway Plan or attend appointments. They linked job creation to free trade agreements with China, Korea, Japan, and the Trans-Pacific Partnership, citing examples of increased agricultural exports from the Mallee electorate, such as 10,000 tonnes of citrus and over 1,000 containers of table grapes to China.

speeches.speaker: Clare O'Neil
speeches.brief: The Labor MP argued that the bill should prioritise job creation for 800,000 unemployed Australians, including one in five young people, and announced support for three provisions that tighten compliance by linking penalties to non-compliance, but opposition to three others deemed punitive and unfair: immediate suspension for not signing a jobs plan, a new penalty for undefined 'inappropriate manner', and removal of the ability to waive penalties for financial hardship.

speeches.speaker: Keith Pitt
speeches.brief: The speaker argued for the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Further Strengthening Job Seeker Compliance) Bill 2015, which extends the no-show no-pay rule to mutual obligation requirements such as entering into a job plan and imposes immediate payment suspensions for noncompliance. He noted that attendance at rescheduled appointments rose from 65% to over 90% after earlier changes, and highlighted unemployment in the Hinkler electorate, citing incentives like a $2,500 job commitment bonus at 12 months and a further $4,000 at 24 months.

speeches.speaker: Eric Hutchinson
speeches.brief: The speaker argued in support of the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Further Strengthening Job Seeker Compliance) Bill 2015, stating it will speed up penalties for non-compliance and improve job seeker engagement, citing attendance rates rising from 65% to over 90% and reduced suspension times. He also highlighted government initiatives including the $13 million Innovation and Investment Fund creating 400 Tasmanian jobs, $60 million for irrigation schemes, $204 million for the Tasmanian Freight Equalisation Scheme, and $5.5 billion small business package, while criticising the member for Denison over shipping policy and welfare waiver provisions.

speeches.speaker: Tony Pasin
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Further Strengthening Job Seeker Compliance) Bill 2015 is needed to rein in government spending by imposing stronger, more immediate penalties on job seekers who refuse suitable work or fail to meet mutual obligations, citing that penalty waivers for refusing work rose from 45% in 2009–10 to 78% in 2013–14 and that the tax-to-GDP ratio is forecast to reach 23.4% by 2018–19, well above the long-term average.

speeches.speaker: Brett Whiteley
speeches.brief: The Social Security Legislation Amendment (Further Strengthening Job Seeker Compliance) Bill 2015 introduces financial penalties for failing to enter an employment pathway plan, for inappropriate behaviour at appointments, and makes penalties more immediate for activities such as Work for the Dole or job interviews. Attendance at reconnection appointments rose from 65% in 2013 to 90% in June 2015, while waiver rates for refusing suitable jobs increased from 45% in 2009–10 to 78% in 2013–14.

speeches.speaker: Mark Coulton
speeches.brief: The speaker argued in support of the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Further Strengthening Job Seeker Compliance) Bill 2015, stating it offers opportunity rather than punishment and helps break intergenerational unemployment. They cited examples from their electorate, including Work for the Dole programs and the Clontarf Foundation in towns like Moree and Coonamble, and asserted that no work is beneath dignity.

speeches.speaker: Barnaby Joyce
speeches.brief: The government argued that the bill will extend immediate payment suspensions and penalties to job seekers who miss specialist appointments, refuse job plans, or make insufficient job search efforts, while removing waivers for eight-week non-payment penalties for refusing suitable work. The bill builds on previous reforms that increased appointment attendance from 65% to over 90% and reduced average payment suspension duration from 5.2 to 3.1 business days.
